progressive-overload.title: Progressive overload: the only 'secret formula' that works
progressive-overload.excerpt: Forget influencer magic routines. If you're not progressing, you're almost certainly ignoring this principle.
content: Every week someone walks into the cave asking for the perfect routine. The answer is always the same: the perfect routine is the one that lets you apply progressive overload consistently for months and years.

Progressive overload is the simplest and most ignored principle in strength training: for your body to adapt, the stimulus must increase over time. More weight, more reps, more sets, better technique or less rest. If everything stays the same for months, your body has no reason to change.

How do you apply it in practice? Keep a log. Yes, that boring and that effective. Write down every set, every weight and every rep. Your goal in each session is to beat — even minimally — what you did in the previous one: one more rep with the same weight, or the same reps with 5 lb more.

The most common mistake is rushing: jumping 20 lb at once, failing, getting frustrated and switching routines. Strength is built with a bricklayer's patience, brick by brick. The strongest lifters in the cave have spent years stacking small increments anyone would consider insignificant.
Start today: pick 4-6 basic exercises, write down your current numbers and commit to improving them by 1% each week. In a year you'll have progressed more than in your entire life of random routines.

protein-myths.title: 5 protein myths holding you back
protein-myths.excerpt: It doesn't wreck your kidneys and you don't need a shake at exactly 30 minutes. We dismantle the bro-science with evidence.
content: Protein is probably the nutrient with the most nonsense spoken about it in any gym. Let's dismantle the five myths we hear most often in the cave.

Myth 1: 'Protein damages your kidneys'. In healthy people, there is no evidence that high protein intake causes kidney damage. The studies that spawned this myth were done on patients with pre-existing kidney disease. If your kidneys work fine, training hard and eating 1 g per pound of body weight won't break them.

Myth 2: 'You only absorb 30 g per meal'. Your body absorbs virtually all the protein you eat; what varies is the speed. To maximize protein synthesis it helps to spread it across 3-5 meals, but if you eat 60 g in one sitting some day, nothing gets 'wasted'.

Myth 3: 'The anabolic window lasts 30 minutes'. The famous post-workout window exists, but it lasts hours, not minutes. What matters is your total daily intake. If you ate protein 2-3 hours before training, there's no rush for the immediate shake.
Myth 4: 'Plant protein is useless'. Plant proteins can be perfectly valid by combining sources (legumes + grains) and adjusting total intake slightly upward. Thousands of vegan athletes prove it.

Myth 5: 'More protein = more muscle'. Above roughly 1 g per pound in a caloric surplus, extra protein doesn't speed up muscle gain. Muscle is built with well-programmed training, enough calories and years of consistency. Protein is the material, not the builder.

first-month-guide.title: Your first month at the gym: a survival guide
first-month-guide.excerpt: Everything we wish we'd known on day one: what to do, what to avoid, and how not to quit in week 3.
content: Half the people who join a gym in January quit before March. Not for lack of motivation, but for lack of a plan. This is the guide we hand every new member of the cave.

Weeks 1-2: learn the patterns, not the weights. Your only goal is mastering the basic movements: squat, hip hinge, push, pull. Use weights that feel ridiculously light. Your nervous system is learning a new language — don't yell at it.

Weeks 3-4: build the habit before the intensity. Three days a week, same days and same time if you can. Mediocre consistency beats intermittent perfection every time. A 60% workout you actually do is worth infinitely more than the perfect workout you skip.
Muscle soreness is normal; joint pain is not. Learn to tell the diffuse next-day muscle ache (fine) from sharp, localized pain in a joint (not fine — stop and ask a coach).
Don't compare your chapter 1 to someone else's chapter 20. The guy squatting 400 lb also started with an empty bar. Nobody in the cave laughs at beginners; we all remember our first day.
And the most important advice: ask for help. That's what the coaches are for. A free initial assessment session saves you months of going in circles and protects you from pointless injuries.

sleep-recovery.title: Sleep more, lift more: the science of recovery
sleep-recovery.excerpt: You train hard but sleep 5 hours. Here's why sleep is the legal steroid you're wasting.
content: You can have the best routine and the best diet in the world: if you sleep badly, you're leaving half your results on the table. Muscle isn't built in the gym — it's built while you sleep.

During deep sleep your body releases most of the day's growth hormone, repairs the muscle tissue damaged by training and consolidates nervous system adaptations. Chronically sleeping less than 6 hours reduces protein synthesis, raises cortisol and tanks testosterone.

The data is scary: studies on athletes show that sleeping 5 hours instead of 8 cuts testosterone levels by 10-15% in just one week. Another classic study found that athletes sleeping under 8 hours had 1.7 times the injury risk.

How to improve your sleep tonight? Fixed schedule (same bedtime and wake time, weekends included), a cold dark room, no screens 60 minutes before bed, and caffeine only before 2 PM. It sounds basic because it is; the hard part is sticking to it.
If you train at night in the cave, prioritize a dinner with carbs and protein, and dim the lights when you get home. Your 9 PM session shouldn't cost you sleep if you manage the following hour well.
Treat sleep like another workout: schedule it, protect it and measure it. It's free, it's legal and it's more anabolic than any supplement on the shelf.
